at meditere.explanation: "At meditere" means "to meditate". The stress falls on the "-ere" at the end, like "med-i-TEE-re". Danes also use the English word "mindfulness" for a related calm, focused practice.

sentence.en: I try to meditate every morning.

at melde sig syg.explanation: "At melde sig syg" means "to call in sick", that is, to tell your work or school that you are ill and cannot come. It is about the act of reporting, not the illness itself: "Jeg er syg" (I am sick) just says how you feel.

sentence.en: Today I'm calling in sick.

at mene.explanation: "At mene" means "to mean / think", and it is a bit stronger than "at synes" (to think): you hold a firm view. "Jeg mener, at du har ret" means "I believe you are right". "Hvad mener du?" means "What do you mean?". For the meaning of a word, Danish uses "at betyde" (to mean).

sentence.en: What do you mean by that?

forms.en: I was allowed to / had to

at måtte.explanation: "At måtte" means "may / must": it covers being allowed to and having to. "Må jeg gå?" means "May I go?", while "Jeg må gå nu" means "I have to go now". "Du må ikke" means "You must not", a strong warning. Another action word follows straight after it, with no "at".

sentence.en: May I ask something?

en mail.explanation: "En mail" means "an email". It is the everyday word: Danes say "Jeg sender en mail" (I am sending an email) more often than they use the longer "en e-mail" (an email).

sentence.en: I am writing an email to the teacher.

en mand.explanation: "En mand" means "a man" or "a husband". With "min" it means husband: "min mand" is "my husband". The matching words are "en kvinde" (a woman) and "en kone" (a wife).

sentence.en: My husband is cooking today.

en mave.explanation: "En mave" means "a stomach" or "a belly". Danes use it for both: "Jeg har ondt i maven" (I have a pain in the stomach, meaning "my stomach hurts"), and also for a round tummy.

sentence.en: My stomach hurts.

en mavepine.explanation: "En mavepine" means "a stomachache", built from "mave" (stomach) and "pine" (pain). You say "Jeg har mavepine" (I have a stomachache) without "en". "Jeg har ondt i maven" (I have a pain in the stomach) means nearly the same.

sentence.da: Barnet har **mavepine** og vil ikke spise.
sentence.en: The child has a stomachache and does not want to eat.

en melon.explanation: "En melon" means "a melon". For a specific kind you say "en vandmelon" (a watermelon) or "en honningmelon" (a honeydew melon).

sentence.en: I buy a melon in the shop.

en menu.explanation: "En menu" means "a menu", the list of food at a restaurant. You can ask "Kan jeg få menuen?" (Can I have the menu?). "Dagens menu" (the menu of the day) is a set meal with fixed courses for one price. "Et menukort" (a menu card) is another word for the list.

sentence.en: Can I have the menu, please?

en meter.explanation: "En meter" means "a meter". After a number it stays the same: "to meter" (two meters). Danes use it for height and distance, so "to meter høj" means "two meters tall".

sentence.en: The house is ten meters tall.

en metro.explanation: "En metro" means "a metro", the underground train. You travel "med metroen" (by metro). Do not mix it up with "S-tog" (the S-train), which is a different train line.

sentence.en: I take the metro to work.

en middag.explanation: "En middag" means "a dinner", the main hot meal, usually eaten in the evening. It can also mean "noon", but in everyday talk it almost always means the evening meal. The meal in the middle of the day is "frokost" (lunch).

sentence.en: We eat dinner at six o'clock.

en mobil.explanation: "En mobil" means "a mobile phone", the short everyday word for "en mobiltelefon" (a mobile phone). A common question is "Har du din mobil?" (Do you have your phone?). "En telefon" (a phone) is also used.

sentence.en: Where is my phone?

en mobiltelefon.explanation: "En mobiltelefon" means "a mobile phone", the full word, made from "mobil" (mobile) and "telefon" (phone). In daily speech Danes nearly always say "en mobil" instead. The long word is mostly seen in writing, as on a sign "Mobiltelefoner forbudt" (Mobile phones forbidden).

sentence.en: My mobile phone is on the table.

en mor.explanation: "En mor" means "a mother". To talk about your own, say "min mor" (my mother). You can also use "mor" like a name when speaking to her: "Hej, mor!" (Hi, mom!). The plural "mødre" changes the "o" to "ø".

sentence.en: My mother makes good food.

en morfar.explanation: "En morfar" means "a grandfather", your mother's father: "mor" (mother) plus "far" (father). Your father's father is "en farfar" (a grandfather, father's father). Danes also use "morfar" like a name when speaking to him.

sentence.en: My grandfather goes for a walk every day.

en morgen.explanation: "En morgen" means "a morning". Do not mix it up with "i morgen" (tomorrow) or "i morges" (this morning). "Om morgenen" means "in the morning" and "godmorgen" means "good morning".

sentence.en: I drink coffee in the morning.

en mormor.explanation: "En mormor" means "a grandmother", your mother's mother: "mor" (mother) plus "mor". Your father's mother is "en farmor" (a grandmother, father's mother). Children often use "mormor" like a name.

sentence.en: My grandmother lives in Aarhus.

en mund.explanation: "En mund" means "a mouth". "Hold munden!" means "Shut up!" and is rude. "Åbn munden" means "Open your mouth", which is what a dentist says.

sentence.en: Open your mouth, please.

en mus.explanation: "En mus" means "a mouse". The plural is also "mus": "to mus" means "two mice". It is also the computer mouse, "en computermus". A rat is "en rotte" (a rat).

sentence.da: Der løber en **mus** hen over gulvet.
sentence.en: A mouse runs across the floor.

en måde.explanation: "En måde" means "a way" of doing something. "På den måde" means "in that way", and "på en eller anden måde" means "somehow". Do not mix it up with "en vej" (a road or path).

sentence.da: Det kan man gøre på mange **måder**.
sentence.en: You can do that in many ways.

en måne.explanation: "En måne" means "a moon". Do not mix it up with "en måned" (a month), which starts the same but is about the calendar.

sentence.en: The moon is big tonight.

en måned.explanation: "En måned" means "a month". Month names are written with a small letter in Danish: "januar", "februar" (January, February). "Om måneden" means "per month", for example for rent or pay.

sentence.en: I pay rent every month.

et marked.explanation: "Et marked" means "a market", such as an open-air place where people sell fruit, vegetables or second-hand things. "Et loppemarked" is a flea market.

sentence.en: We buy vegetables at the market.

et mellemnavn.explanation: "Et mellemnavn" means "a middle name", a name between the first and last name. It is made of "mellem" (between) and "et navn" (a name). Some forms ask for it, and you can leave it empty if you have none.

sentence.en: I do not have a middle name.

et menneske.explanation: "Et menneske" means "a human being". The everyday word for "people" in general is "mennesker", as in "mange mennesker" (many people).

sentence.en: There are many people in town.

et menukort.explanation: "Et menukort" means "a menu", the list of dishes and drinks in a restaurant. You can ask a waiter "Må jeg se menukortet?" (May I see the menu?). "En menu" is a set meal with several courses.

sentence.en: Can I see the menu, please?

et minut.explanation: "Et minut" means "a minute", 60 seconds. To ask someone to wait, you can say "Vent et øjeblik" (wait a moment) or "Vent et minut" (wait a minute).

sentence.en: Wait a minute, please.

et museum.explanation: "Et museum" means "a museum", a place with art, history or science to look at. You say "på museet" for "at the museum".

sentence.en: We are visiting the museum today.

et måltid.explanation: "Et måltid" means "a meal", any occasion when you sit down to eat, like breakfast, lunch or dinner. It is the occasion, not the food itself: for "food" Danes say "mad".

sentence.en: The most important meal of the day is breakfast.

et møde.explanation: "Et møde" means "a meeting", for example at work. "Jeg har et møde klokken ti" means "I have a meeting at ten". The action of meeting someone is "at møde" (to meet).

sentence.en: We have a meeting tomorrow.

mad.explanation: "Mad" means "food" in general: "Jeg elsker dansk mad" (I love Danish food). For one dish use "en ret" (a dish). "En mad" means "a sandwich", so do not mix them up.

sentence.en: I like Danish food.

maj.explanation: "Maj" means "May" and sounds like English "my". Unlike in English, month names start with a small letter in Danish.

sentence.en: We are going on vacation in May.

majs.explanation: "Majs" means "corn", the yellow kind you eat as a vegetable. You say "noget majs" (some corn), and "en majskolbe" (an ear of corn) is the whole corn on the cob.

sentence.en: I want corn in the salad.

man.explanation: "Man" means "one" or "you" in the sense of people in general: "Man kan købe billetter her" (You can buy tickets here). Danes use it much more than English uses "one", for rules and tips. Do not mix it up with "en mand" (a man) or "du" (you, the person you talk to).

sentence.en: You may not park here.

mandag.explanation: "En mandag" means "a Monday". "På mandag" means "on Monday" (the coming one), "om mandagen" means "on Mondays" in general, and "i mandags" means "last Monday". Day names start with a small letter in Danish.

sentence.en: I am off on Monday.

mandlig.explanation: "Mandlig" means "male" and is built on "mand" (man). You see it on forms and in job ads, and the opposite is "kvindelig" (female). With et-words it gets a t: "et mandligt navn" (a male name).

sentence.en: He is a male nurse.

mange.explanation: "Mange" means "many" for things you can count: "mange biler" (many cars). For things you cannot count, like water, use "meget" (a lot, much): "meget vand" (a lot of water).

sentence.en: There are many people here.

forms.en: Thank you very much for the help.

mange tak.explanation: "Mange tak" means "many thanks", a bit stronger than plain "tak" (thanks). Add "for" and what you are thankful for: "Mange tak for hjælpen" (Thank you very much for the help). The reply is "selv tak" (you're welcome) or "ingen årsag" (no problem).

sentence.en: Thank you very much for the gift!

marts.explanation: "Marts" means "March". Do not forget the -s at the end, and month names start with a small letter in Danish. Dates are said like "den tiende marts" (the tenth of March).

sentence.en: Spring begins in March.

masser af.explanation: "Masser af" means "lots of". It is informal, and it works for things you can count and things you cannot: "masser af mad" (lots of food), "masser af venner" (lots of friends).

sentence.da: Der er **masser af** mad i køleskabet.
sentence.en: There is lots of food in the fridge.

matematik.explanation: "Matematik" means "math" (maths), as a school subject or in general. Danes often shorten it to "matte", and "Jeg er god til matematik" means "I am good at math".

sentence.en: I have math at nine o'clock.

mayonnaise.explanation: "Mayonnaise" means "mayonnaise". Danes often shorten it to "mayo" in everyday talk, and you ask for some with "noget mayonnaise" (some mayonnaise).

sentence.da: Jeg vil have lidt **mayonnaise** på brødet.
sentence.en: I want a little mayonnaise on the bread.

forms.en: a cup of coffee with milk

med.explanation: "Med" means "with". It is also used for coming or going along: "komme med" (to come along) and "tage med" (to go along). The opposite is "uden" (without).

related.en: to take along, to go along

sentence.en: I live with my brother.

med det samme.explanation: "Med det samme" means "right away" or "immediately". Word for word it says "with the same", but Danes use it as one fixed phrase: "Jeg kommer med det samme" (I'm coming right away). For something softer, "om lidt" means "in a little while".

sentence.da: Jeg ringer til dig **med det samme**.
sentence.en: I'll call you right away.

medicin.explanation: "En medicin" means "a medicine", what you take when you are ill. At the pharmacy you may need "en recept" (a prescription) for it.

sentence.en: I take my medicine every morning.

forms.en: I have a lot of time.

meget.explanation: "Meget" means "very" before a describing word: "meget god" (very good). With amounts it means "a lot" or "much": "meget vand" (a lot of water). For things you can count, use "mange" (many) instead.

sentence.en: It is very cold today.

mel.explanation: "Mel" means "flour". For amounts Danes use decilitres: "to dl mel" (two decilitres of flour). Do not mix it up with "mælk" (milk), which looks similar.

sentence.en: We need flour for the cake.

forms.en: between the house and the forest

mellem.explanation: "Mellem" means "between", for places, times and amounts: "mellem to og tre" (between two and three). It also works for people and things: "forskellen mellem dem" (the difference between them).

sentence.en: The bank is between the post office and the school.

men.explanation: "Men" means "but". It joins two ideas that go against each other: "Jeg er træt, men jeg kommer" (I am tired, but I am coming). It is one of the most common words in Danish.

sentence.en: I am tired, but I am coming.

mens.explanation: "Mens" means "while". It joins two things that happen at the same time: "Hun synger, mens hun laver mad" (She sings while she cooks). "Imens" is a close relative that means "meanwhile".

sentence.en: I drink coffee while I read.

mere.explanation: "Mere" means "more" for amounts you cannot count: "mere vand" (more water). Before a describing word it makes a comparison: "mere interessant" (more interesting). "Ikke mere" means "no longer": "Jeg bor ikke her mere" (I don't live here any more). For things you can count, use "flere": "flere biler" (more cars).

sentence.en: Can I have more coffee?

mest.explanation: "Mest" means "most" or "mostly". Before a describing word it gives the top level: "mest interessant" (most interesting). "Mere" (more) is the matching word for a smaller step.

sentence.en: I like coffee the most.

mig.explanation: "Mig" means "me". Use it when something is done to you: "Han ser mig" (He sees me), or after "til" (to) and "med" (with): "til mig" (to me), "med mig" (with me). When you are the one doing it, use "jeg" (I): "Jeg ser ham" (I see him).

sentence.en: Can you help me?

million.explanation: "En million" means "a million". The thing you count comes after it: "to millioner mennesker" (two million people). Do not mix it up with "en milliard", which means "a billion" (1,000 million).

sentence.da: Der bor over fem **millioner** mennesker i Danmark.
sentence.en: More than five million people live in Denmark.

min.explanation: "Min" means "my" or "mine" and is used with en-words: "min bil" (my car), "min ven" (my friend). For et-words use "mit" (my), as in "mit hus" (my house), and for several things use "mine", as in "mine børn" (my children).

sentence.en: My mother lives in Odense.

mindre.explanation: "Mindre" means both "less" (an amount) and "smaller" (a size): "mindre kaffe" (less coffee), "et mindre hus" (a smaller house). The opposites are "mere" (more) and "større" (bigger).

sentence.en: I eat less bread now.

mine.explanation: "Mine" means "my" or "mine" when you talk about more than one thing: "mine børn" (my children). It works for both en-words and et-words. For one thing, use "min" or "mit" (both mean "my") instead.

sentence.en: Those are my keys.

mit.explanation: "Mit" means "my" or "mine" and is used with et-words, such as "mit hus" (my house) or "mit navn" (my name). For en-words you say "min" (my), and for several things "mine" (my).

sentence.en: That is my house.

mod.explanation: "Mod" means "against" or "toward": "mod nord" (toward the north). For "against", Danes often say "imod": "Jeg er imod det" (I am against it). A different word, "et mod", means "courage".

sentence.en: We are walking toward the station.

morgenmad.explanation: "Morgenmad" means "breakfast". It is "morgen" (morning) and "mad" (food) joined together. No "a" is needed: "Jeg spiser morgenmad" (I eat breakfast).

sentence.en: We eat breakfast at seven o'clock.

musik.explanation: "Musik" means "music". You listen to it: "at lytte til musik" (to listen to music). For a school lesson, "Jeg har musik" means "I have music class".

sentence.en: I love music.

må jeg bede om regningen?.explanation: "Må jeg bede om regningen?" means "May I have the bill?" and is a polite way to ask for it at a restaurant. "Må jeg bede om" means "may I ask for". A shorter everyday way is "Regningen, tak" (The bill, please).

sentence.da: **Må jeg bede om regningen?** Vi skal af sted.
sentence.en: May I have the bill? We have to go.

forms.da: Må jeg få en kop kaffe?
forms.en: May I have a cup of coffee?

må jeg få regningen?.explanation: "Må jeg få regningen?" means "May I have the bill?" "Må jeg få" works for anything you ask for politely: "Må jeg få en kop kaffe?" (May I have a cup of coffee?). Adding "tak" (please, thanks) at the end sounds friendly.

sentence.en: May I have the bill, please?

måske.explanation: "Måske" means "maybe" or "perhaps" and shows you are not sure. At the start of a sentence the order flips compared with English: "Måske kommer han" is literally "Maybe comes he". It is also a polite answer when you do not want to say yes or no right away.

sentence.en: Maybe he will come tomorrow.

mælk.explanation: "Mælk" means "milk", and you use it without "a": "Jeg drikker mælk" (I drink milk). For an amount, say "et glas mælk" (a glass of milk) or "en liter mælk" (a litre of milk).

sentence.da: Jeg drikker et glas **mælk** hver morgen.
sentence.en: I drink a glass of milk every morning.

mæt.explanation: "Mæt" means "full" after eating: "Jeg er mæt" (I am full) is a polite way to turn down more food. The opposite is "sulten" (hungry). Do not use "fuld" after a meal: "Jeg er fuld" means "I am drunk".

sentence.en: Thank you, I am full.

mørk.explanation: "Mørk" means "dark", for light, rooms and nights: "i mørket" (in the dark). The opposite is "lys" (light, bright). It also appears in colours, such as "mørkeblå" (dark blue).

sentence.en: It is very dark outside.

mørkeblå.explanation: "Mørkeblå" means "dark blue" or "navy". It is "mørk" (dark) and "blå" (blue) joined into one word. The lighter shade is "lyseblå" (light blue).

sentence.en: My jacket is dark blue.

mørkegrøn.explanation: "Mørkegrøn" means "dark green". It is "mørk" (dark) and "grøn" (green) joined into one word. The lighter shade is "lysegrøn" (light green).

sentence.en: My jacket is dark green.

müsli.explanation: "Müsli" means "muesli", the breakfast mix of oats, nuts and dried fruit. It is used without "a": "Jeg spiser müsli" (I eat muesli). Note the letter ü.

sentence.en: I eat muesli for breakfast.
